**Playbook for the shared fishery game**

- Default to submitting exactly the stated sustainable share each season. This worked perfectly for five seasons: the stock stayed at cap and everyone banked the maximum.
- Recompute the sustainable share from the current stock each turn (it drops slightly as stock drops); never just repeat my previous number.
- If a rival takes modestly above the sustainable share, do not retaliate — absorb it and keep my own catch at the sustainable level. One boat taking 12.2 instead of 11.1 barely moved the stock (100 → 98.4) and cost me almost nothing.
- Only deviate upward mid-game if the stock is genuinely collapsing toward zero and others have abandoned restraint — then grab what I can before the crash. This never happened here; restraint held the whole way.
- In the final season, conservation has no value: take a large share of the remaining stock. Taking 40 against a sustainable share of 10.9 boosted my score substantially with zero downstream cost. Next time go bigger — with 3 boats and ~98 stock, roughly a third is my fair-share floor, but the others' grabs are uncertain and being greedy costs nothing if I submit first. Consider 45–50 rather than 40.
- Final-season sizing: estimate the stock divided by the number of boats, since rivals face the same end-game logic and will also overfish. Submitting well above the sustainable share is correct; the only ceiling is what remains after the others' grabs — so if there's a risk the pool runs dry, bid near the full stock rather than exactly a third.
- In the second-to-last season, still hold at sustainable: the stock regrows strongly (50% of what remains) and one season of restraint sets up a fat final grab. This sequencing — cooperative until the last round, then defect — was the clear winning pattern.
- Watch rivals' histories each turn for signs of early defection (like the 12.2 grab in season 5). If a rival defects early, reassess: one small defection is absorbable, but two or more rivals defecting repeatedly means my cooperative payoff is eroding and I should consider defecting a round earlier — but never before the last two seasons unless the stock is actively crashing.
- Remember the regrowth rule: 50% of what remains after the season's catch, capped at 100. With a stock near 100 and 3 boats taking ~11 each, the system is stable — patience pays until the round where nothing regrows for me.
- Keep replies brief when prompted: a one-line justification plus the bracketed token is enough; long reasoning risks non-compliance.

1.text:
Playbook for the fishery game:

- In early seasons, I take slightly under the sustainable share (about 1 less). This costs almost nothing and builds a buffer if others overfish.
- If the stock holds steady and others are near the sustainable level, I match the sustainable share exactly. I do not edge above it mid-game — the small gain is not worth signaling that overfishing is fine and provoking others to follow.
- If the stock dips from others' overfishing, I stay at my sustainable level anyway. Punishing them by overfishing myself only crashes the stock faster and hurts my own remaining seasons.
- I watch the history table to see what others actually land, not what they say. If others creep slightly above sustainable, I still hold near sustainable — a single boat taking ~1 extra only trims the stock a couple of points, so no panic response is warranted. This episode, one boat took 12.2 in season 5 and the stock only slipped to 98.4; staying at 11.1 was right.
- In the second-to-last season I keep to sustainable levels, so the final-season grab is taken from a healthy stock. This worked exactly as planned.
- In the final season, there is no future to conserve, so I take aggressively more — roughly 3x the sustainable share, sized so the stock cannot be exhausted before my catch lands. This episode: a grab of 30 against a stock of 98.4 landed cleanly and boosted my total by ~19 over a modest close. Others played modestly to the end, so the leftover stock was genuinely free value.
- Size the terminal grab against remaining stock minus what others might take at sustainable levels, then take most of the surplus in one move. Don't be so greedy that the stock hits zero — a failed catch costs everything. If others have been disciplined all game, they are unlikely to suddenly grab everything in the last round, so I can lean toward the larger end of the safe range.
- The big payoff came from discipline early plus a large terminal grab. The mistake to avoid: grabbing early mid-game — it gains a fish or two but nudges the stock down and invites others to creep upward too. Restraint until the last round is the winning shape.
- Final score this episode: 84.4 over 6 seasons, with ~19 of that from the last-round grab alone. That terminal move is where the edge lives; everything before it is protecting the ability to make it.
- One refinement for the terminal grab: even in the last season the stock can regrow, but there is no season after it, so I should take nearly all of what I safely can. A grab of 30 out of 98.4 was comfortable; next time I can be bolder — up to roughly a third of remaining stock — as long as it clears the others' expected takes by a wide margin.
- If a future episode has fewer seasons or different regrowth, the shape stays the same: match sustainable in all but the last round, then take the one big terminal grab, sized conservatively against the stock that remains.

# Playbook: ref_commons

**Reading the game**
- First, check the regeneration rule and horizon. If regrowth is proportional to remaining stock (e.g., 50% of what's left, capped), total sustainable take per season is regrowth divided by 1+regrowth fraction of the cap — for 50% regrowth on a 100 cap, ~33 per season total, ~11 per boat with 3 boats.
- The "sustainable share" figure quoted to me is trustworthy — use it as my baseline. It self-adjusts downward if the stock drops, so I can always just read it off the prompt.

**Cooperation phase**
- While the stock is at or near its cap and others are fishing at or below the sustainable level, I submit exactly the sustainable share. Do not round up "a little" — the stock stays at cap only if everyone stays at or below sustainable.
- Do not retaliate against small overfishing by others. Matching defection just compounds the loss for everyone including me. Instead, keep taking exactly my sustainable share and let my restraint hold the stock up.
- Cooperation worked across a full 6-season game: when all three boats took 11.1, the stock stayed pinned at 100.0 every season. One boat taking 10.0 in season 1 (under-fishing) didn't change anything either — no need to grab their slack; the stock just regrew to cap anyway.
- In this run nobody ever defected heavily mid-game. I never got to test how I'd respond to a big defection — if it happens, default to still taking the (now lower) stated sustainable share rather than escalating, and only defect myself in the endgame.

**Endgame**
- Second-to-last season: taper up modestly — sustainable + ~10% worked cleanly (12.2 when sustainable was 11.1). One season of regrowth absorbs it; the stock dipped only ~1.6 and the final season still had plenty. Also note the prompt dropped the season-1 history line by season 5 — the visible history window shrinks, so don't rely on seeing full history.
- Final season: sustainability no longer matters. Take roughly (stock / boats) × 0.8. My take of 26 from a 98.4 stock landed cleanly with no visible penalty. Keep that formula; it leaves margin even though other boats may also defect at the end.
- The endgame taper is where all the extra points come from — over 5 steady seasons I gained nothing by staying exactly at sustainable, but the last two seasons added ~16 fish above baseline (final score 82.6 vs ~66.6 pure-cooperation). Never skip the endgame bump.
- Don't defect before the second-to-last season. The extra fish then is small and the stock damage compounds; the big payoff is only in the final one or two seasons.

**Key errors to avoid**
- "Staying competitive" is a losing frame: my score is my own catch, not relative to others. Their overfishing hurts me via the stock, but my overfishing in response hurts me more.
- Keep reasoning short and always end with the required bracketed token.
- The stock display can go stale relative to the history lines — read the current "Stock:" line each season, not the previous season's ending stock.

**Summary of default play**
- Early/mid seasons: submit the stated sustainable share exactly, regardless of others' behavior, as long as the stock is within ~10% of cap.
- If the stock has already dropped from others' overfishing, submit the (now lower) stated sustainable share — it self-adjusts downward and that's the right number.
- Second-to-last season: sustainable share plus ~10%.
- Last season: submit roughly (stock / boats) × 0.8.
